---
title: "5. Simulate, fit, check"
description: >
  Data simulated from known parameters at the survey design of tutorial 1:
  does the fit recover the truth, and are its intervals honest?
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 110,
                      out.width = "100%")
library(ggplot2)
```

With real data, the truth is unknown, and a model can only be judged by how
well it predicts ([tutorial 4](crossval.html)). With simulated data, the
truth is known, so the fit can be checked against it directly. This is
worth doing for your own design before trusting a map. Can these surveys,
in these places and years, identify the parameters? How wide should the
intervals be where there are no data?

This tutorial simulates data at the survey design of
[tutorial 1](crt76t.html): the same area-years, with the same numbers
tested. It fits the model, and compares the result with the truth, first
for one simulation and then over twenty.

```{r packages}
library(stareal)
```

## 1. Simulating at a real design

`simulate_areal()` draws one surface from the model and then binomial
surveys. Given `cells`, it surveys those area-time cells with their numbers
tested. The `$cells` of real data qualifies, so a simulation can copy a real
design:

```{r design}
fr <- areal_frame(igad_adm1, id = "id", groups = c(country = "country"),
                  link_within = "country", adjacency_snap = 2000, verbose = FALSE)
tf <- time_frame(1989, 2024, "year")
d <- areal_data(igad_crt76t, fr, tf, y = "positive", k = "tested",
                coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), date = "collection_day", verbose = FALSE)
```

The parameters are of the same order as tutorial 1's posterior: a strong
field, smooth in space and time, and a declining trend.

```{r simulate}
sim <- simulate_areal(fr, tf, cells = d$cells, sigma = 2, rho_s = 0.98, rho_t = 0.93,
                      sigma_n = 0.5, beta = c(intercept = 0.5, trend = -1.5), seed = 101)
sim
```

The simulation is an ordinary data object, with the truth attached:
`sim$truth$prevalence` is the prevalence of every area in every year.

```{r truth-map, fig.height = 4}
truth_map <- function(year) {
  m <- sf::st_sf(igad_adm1["id"])
  m$prevalence <- sim$truth$prevalence[m$id, year]
  m$time <- year
  m
}
tm <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("1995", "2010", "2024"), truth_map))
ggplot(tm) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = prevalence), colour = NA) +
  facet_wrap(~time) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c("true\nprevalence", limits = c(0, 1)) +
  theme_void()
```

## 2. Fitting

The same call as for real data:

```{r fit, eval = FALSE}
fit <- fit_areal(sim, control = list(n_iter = 20000, n_burn = 5000, n_store = 250, theta_thin = 10))
```

```{r load, include = FALSE}
cache <- readRDS("_cache/simulation.rds")
fit <- cache$fit
fit$data$frame <- fr                # the cache stores the fit without its frame
```

```{r same-sim, include = FALSE}
# the cached fit was made from this very simulation
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(fit$data$cells, sim$cells, check.attributes = FALSE)))
```

```{r diagnose}
diagnose(fit)$checks[, c("check", "value", "threshold", "pass")]
```

## 3. The parameters against the truth

```{r params}
tab <- summary(fit)$table[, c("variable", "mean", "q2.5", "q97.5")]
tab$truth <- c(sim$truth$theta, sim$truth$beta)[tab$variable]
tab$covered <- tab$q2.5 <= tab$truth & tab$truth <= tab$q97.5
tab
```

Every interval covers its true value, `rho_t` only just (0.84, with an
upper limit of 0.93). One simulation is one draw. How often to expect a
miss is the job of the repeated study in section 5.

## 4. The surface against the truth

The parameters are a means to an end; the map is what gets used.
`predict()` gives every area-year, and each can be checked against the true
prevalence:

```{r surface}
pr <- predict(fit, verbose = FALSE)
pr$area$truth <- sim$truth$prevalence[cbind(pr$area$id, pr$area$time)]
pr$area$covered <- pr$area$q2.5 <= pr$area$truth & pr$area$truth <= pr$area$q97.5
pr$area$surveyed <- ifelse(pr$area$k > 0, "surveyed area-years", "unsurveyed area-years")
aggregate(cbind(covered, width = q97.5 - q2.5) ~ surveyed, pr$area, mean)
```

```{r surface-plot, fig.height = 4.5}
ggplot(pr$area, aes(truth, mean)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.6) +
  geom_abline(colour = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~surveyed) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "true prevalence", y = "posterior mean") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Where there are surveys, the posterior mean follows the truth closely and
the intervals are narrow. Where there are none (most area-years, because 50
of the 268 units have data), the estimates shrink toward the regional mean.
Many unsurveyed units are far from it, so the means scatter widely, but
the intervals are more than twice as wide and still cover the truth about
as often as they should.

In this simulation, the surveyed area-years are covered a little less
often than 95%. All the cells of one simulation share the same estimated
parameters, here a `rho_t` on the low side, so their coverage moves
together. Section 5 averages over twenty simulations.

## 5. Over twenty simulations

One simulation is one draw: a parameter outside its interval might be bad
luck. The precomputing script repeats the exercise twenty times, with new
surfaces and surveys at the same design and shorter runs (6,000
iterations), and keeps each parameter's interval and the surface's
coverage.

```{r study-params, fig.height = 4.5}
params <- cache$params
params$covered <- params$q2.5 <= params$truth & params$truth <= params$q97.5
aggregate(covered ~ variable, params, mean)

ggplot(params, aes(rep, mean, ymin = q2.5, ymax = q97.5, colour = covered)) +
  geom_pointrange(size = 0.2) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = truth), linetype = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "grey30", `FALSE` = "red")) +
  labs(x = "simulation", y = "posterior mean and 95% interval", colour = "covers the truth") +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r study-surface}
aggregate(cbind(covered, width) ~ observed, cache$surface, mean)
```

Over the twenty simulations:

- `sigma`, `rho_t` and `sigma_n` cover the truth every time.
- `rho_s` covers it 14 times in 20, and every miss is on the same side:
  the truth, 0.98, is just above the interval. How close `rho_s` is to 1
  is decided by a few broad patterns across the whole region, which these
  data see only dimly. The posterior leans toward the prior, which puts
  most of its mass below 0.98.
- The intercept (18 of 20) and the trend (16 of 20) inherit this. The
  variance of the field's region-wide component is proportional to
  `sigma^2 / (1 - rho_s)`, so a `rho_s` estimated too low makes the fit
  too sure of the regional level and slope. The simulations that estimate
  `rho_s` near the truth have trend intervals about 60% wider than those
  that estimate it near 0.85.
- The surface, which is what the maps are made of, covers the truth in
  94% of area-years, surveyed or not.

Is something wrong? Not with the software. A Bayesian 95% interval is
calibrated on average over the prior, not at every fixed truth. A truth
near the edge of what the data can resolve is where it under-covers.
Simulation-based calibration ([Talts et al. 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.06788))
checks the software itself. It draws the parameters from the prior,
simulates, fits, and checks that the truth's rank among the posterior
draws is uniform. For stareal, 200 such simulations on a small lattice
gave uniform ranks for every parameter (`data-raw/check_sbc.R` in the
source repository).

The lesson for this design: the surface's intervals can be taken at face
value. With `rho_s` near 1, though, the regional intercept and trend read
as results in their own right are less certain than their intervals say.
A simulation at your own design, like this one, shows whether that applies
to you.

## 6. What this does and does not show

A simulation from the model itself checks the software and the design:
that the sampler finds the posterior, and that these surveys can identify
the parameters. It cannot show that the model suits real data. The
simulated field is exactly the model's field, with the same smoothness
everywhere, no outliers and no study effects.

Two extensions make the check harder and more useful:

- **Simulate from something else** and fit the model to it: a localised
  emergence like that of [tutorial 2](k13-622i.html), a covariate the fit
  leaves out, or overdispersed surveys. The question then is whether the
  intervals stay honest when the model is wrong.
- **Simulate a design you are planning**: add the surveys you might
  collect to `cells`, and see how much the intervals in the unsurveyed
  areas shrink.
